title: Micah
lead: Micah of Moresheth, a prophet of the Shephelah in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (about 750 to 686 BC), and the book that bears his name: seven chapters of poetry in three rounds that each begin "Hear" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) and move from judgment to hope.

sections.b: Micah is called "of Moresheth" (1:1), a town in the Shephelah, the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, near Gath (1:14). His name is a short form of Mikayahu, "Who is like the LORD?", and the book ends on that question (7:18). Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12 as a word spoken in the days of Hezekiah and says Hezekiah did not kill him but feared the LORD. He prophesied about Samaria and Jerusalem during the Assyrian rise: the fall of Samaria in 722/721 BC and Sennacherib's invasion in 701.

Three rounds, each beginning "Hear": chapters 1 to 2 (judgment on Samaria and Judah's land-grabbers, ending with a promise of gathering), chapters 3 to 5 (judgment on rulers and prophets, ending with Zion exalted and a ruler from Bethlehem), chapters 6 to 7 (the LORD's lawsuit, a lament and a closing praise of the God who pardons). The book moves from judgment to hope three times. Whether the hopeful parts are Micah's or later is a main question of the critical study of the book.

The book holds some of the most quoted lines of the Old Testament: the nations beating swords into plowshares (4:3), the ruler from Bethlehem (5:2, quoted in Matthew 2:5-6), and what the LORD requires: to do justice, love loyal love and walk humbly with God (6:8).
